conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Ramirez, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers adjust emotionally after birth. Today I’d like to sit with you for a few minutes and use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short—to get a clearer picture of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply a screening tool that looks at mood, anxiety, and coping during the first postpartum weeks; it isn’t a test you can “pass” or “fail.” Everything you share is confidential, and my only goal is to support you and make sure you’re not facing these early motherhood ups and downs alone.

We’ll go through 10 questions about the past seven days. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember numbers or options, just tell me what feels true for you. If any question feels hard, we can pause or come back to it. Ready to begin?

1) In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, I’ve noticed that laughing feels kind of forced lately. When my partner tries to joke around, I give a little smile, but I don’t feel that spark of joy like I used to. It’s like I’m too tired or worried to really let go and laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I can fake a chuckle if someone says something funny, but it feels flat, like I’m just going through the motions. Most of the time I don’t even feel like trying.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much anymore. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels kind of “why bother.” I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not reading his cues right or I’m a “bad mom.” I know in my head that babies just cry, but the guilt still pops up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often, actually. Even when everything looks fine—the baby’s sleeping, the house is quiet—my mind keeps spinning with “what-ifs.” I’ll lie there wondering if he’s breathing okay or if I’ll accidentally trip while holding him. I can’t always point to a real reason; the worry just shows up and sticks around.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week my heart just started racing out of nowhere, like I was about to get bad news, but nothing was happening. I’d be changing his diaper and suddenly feel shaky and short-of-breath. It passes if I walk around and breathe slowly, but it’s scary while it lasts.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the minute I finish one feed, the next is due, or there’s laundry piled up and I haven’t eaten a real meal. I keep telling myself it’s normal with a newborn, but sometimes I just want to sit in the closet and cry because it feels like I’ll never catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off—running through everything I might have messed up or need to do tomorrow. I finally drift off, then I jolt awake at every little sound he makes, heart pounding. Some nights I’m awake two or three times for an hour each.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time, yeah. It’s not always crying-level sad—more like this heavy, gray cloud. I’ll be feeding him and just feel empty, like I’m watching someone else’s life. The sadness comes and goes, but it’s definitely there most days.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Once or twice this week I just broke down—yesterday after he finally napped and the house was quiet, I sat on the couch and bawled. It’s not all-day crying, but when it hits, it feels like a wave I can’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… I’ve had a couple of quick flashes, like “what if I just didn’t wake up,” but they’re gone as fast as they come. I don’t have any plan or real wish to do it—I’m too scared of leaving my baby—but the thought has popped in, maybe twice this week.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≤12 wks)  

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent tearfulness  
- Unwarranted self-blame/guilt re parenting competence  
- Marked generalized anxiety and nocturnal worry, 2–3 panic episodes this week  
- Sleep disruption (initial and middle insomnia) directly linked to ruminative mood  
- Chronic feeling overwhelmed, “never catch up”  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan, intent, or protective omission)  

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate–severe depressive and comorbid anxiety symptoms emerging post-birth; functional impact moderate–high; safety risk present (passive SI) but denied active intent.  

Screening significance  
Elevated probability for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid Anxiety Disorder. Safety assessment required now; referral for comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and support services indicated.
